description: Special and general revelation, visions, enlightenment, divine attributes, and challenges to religious experience.
content_html:
How Do People Claim to Know God?

If God exists, how might humans gain knowledge of this? Religious traditions across the world describe two broad paths: special revelation and general revelation. Both have been used to describe divine attributes — the qualities believers ascribe to God. Both have also been challenged by philosophers and non-believers. This lesson explores what these terms mean, what they reveal about the divine, and why their value is contested.

Special Revelation: Visions

Special revelation refers to direct, personal experiences in which God (or, in non-theistic traditions, ultimate reality) is believed to communicate with a specific individual. One of the most commonly cited forms is the vision. Visions are reported across religious traditions. In Christianity, the conversion of Saul on the road to Damascus (Acts 9) is a classic example: Saul was travelling to persecute Christians when a blinding light surrounded him and he heard the voice of Jesus. After this experience, he became Paul the Apostle and one of the most significant figures in early Christianity. Believers regard this as a direct encounter with the risen Christ — a special revelation that transformed an individual’s life and understanding.

The Marian apparitions at Lourdes in 1858 offer a second example. The 14-year-old Bernadette Soubirous reported seeing a vision of a luminous woman at the grotto of Massabielle near Lourdes who identified herself as “the Immaculate Conception.” The Catholic Church, after extensive investigation, officially recognised the apparitions in 1862. The site of Lourdes has since become one of the world’s most visited pilgrimage destinations, and the healings reported there are subject to scrutiny by a medical bureau. For Catholics, Bernadette’s vision is a genuine revelation — a direct communication from the divine to a human being.

Key Fact

Two widely cited examples of visions: (1) Saul on the road to Damascus (Acts 9) — a blinding light and the voice of Jesus led to Saul’s conversion and transformation into Paul the Apostle. (2) Bernadette Soubirous at Lourdes (1858) — visions of the Virgin Mary, recognised by the Catholic Church, that established Lourdes as a major pilgrimage site.

Special Revelation: Enlightenment

Enlightenment is a distinct category of special revelation that appears across several traditions. In Buddhism, the Bodhi (awakening) of Siddhartha Gautama under the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya is the paradigmatic example. The Buddha did not receive a revelation from a creator God — Buddhism does not require belief in such a God — but he attained a direct insight into the nature of reality: the Four Noble Truths and the way to end suffering. This is significant for Theme C because it illustrates how the idea of “revelation” operates differently in different traditions. For Buddhists, enlightenment is the direct realisation of truth about existence, not a message from a divine person.

In Sikh teaching, the founder Guru Nanak received a revelation from Waheguru (God) when he went to bathe in a river and did not return for three days. When he emerged, he declared: “There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.” Sikhs understand this as a direct divine revelation that formed the foundation of the Sikh path. The Guru Granth Sahib, the eternal Sikh scripture, is itself understood as the living word of God — revelation in written form. In Hindu mystical traditions such as Advaita Vedanta, the highest form of enlightenment (moksha) involves the direct experiential realisation that atman (the individual self) and Brahman (ultimate reality) are one.

General Revelation: Nature and Scripture

Unlike special revelation (which comes to specific individuals), general revelation is available to all people through the natural world and through reason. Many believers hold that the beauty and order of nature — the turning of seasons, the complexity of the cell, the vastness of the cosmos — communicates something about its creator. The Christian theologian Thomas Aquinas believed that natural reason could arrive at some knowledge of God through the created order, even without scripture. The Qur’an calls the natural world “ayat” (signs) of God’s existence and power: “In the creation of the heavens and earth... there are signs for those who reason” (Qur’an 3:190). Genesis 1 presents God as deliberately ordering creation: “God saw all that he had made, and it was very good” (Genesis 1:31), suggesting that creation itself reflects God’s character.

Scripture is another form of general revelation that believers across traditions regard as a source of knowledge about the divine. The Christian Bible, the Qur’an, the Torah, and the Guru Granth Sahib are each regarded by their respective communities as containing revealed knowledge of God’s nature, will and purposes. For many believers, scripture provides a more reliable and systematic form of knowledge about God than individual mystical experience, precisely because it is accessible to all and tested by a community over time.

Religious traditions describe the divine using several key attributes. An omnipotent God has unlimited power — a quality supported by accounts of miracles and by the creation narratives in Genesis, the Qur’an and the Guru Granth Sahib. An omniscient God knows all things, including the deepest thoughts of every human being — present in Psalm 139 (“You have searched me, Lord, and you know me”) and in Islamic teaching about God’s omniscience (al-Alim).

Theistic traditions also distinguish between a personal God — one who cares for individuals, hears prayer, and acts in history — and an impersonal divine — an ultimate reality or force that does not relate to humans as a person. Many Hindu schools understand Brahman as ultimately impersonal: the ground of all existence, not a deity with feelings or intentions. Buddhism similarly does not teach a personal creator God. By contrast, Christianity, Islam, Judaism and Sikhism all describe God in strongly personal terms.

A immanent God is present within the world and within human experience: active in history, responsive to prayer, encountered in worship. A transcendent God exists beyond and above the universe: unlimited by space, time or matter. Most monotheistic traditions hold that God is both — “closer to you than your jugular vein” (Qur’an 50:16) and yet beyond full human comprehension. The tension between divine immanence and transcendence is a central theme in the philosophy of religion.

Challenges to Revelation as a Source of Knowledge

Not everyone accepts that visions, miracles and religious experiences are genuine sources of knowledge about the divine. Several challenges deserve careful consideration. First, different revelatory experiences lead to contradictory conclusions about the divine — some describe a personal God, others an impersonal ultimate reality, others a universe without any creator at all. If revelation were a reliable source of knowledge, we might expect greater agreement. Philosophers such as John Hick have grappled with this, arguing that all religious experiences may be culturally shaped encounters with the same ultimate reality.

Second, there is always the possibility that those who claim to have had visions or miraculous experiences were lying or mistaken. Hume argued that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and personal testimony — especially from centuries ago — does not meet this standard. Modern psychology offers natural explanations for mystical experiences: they may result from unusual brain states, sensory deprivation, grief, or temporal lobe activity. The philosopher Ludwig Feuerbach argued that “God” is a human projection — what we value most in ourselves, projected onto the cosmos.

Humanists and atheists typically hold that reported visions and religious experiences, however sincere, do not provide reliable evidence of an objective divine reality. They point out that the specific content of religious experiences consistently reflects the cultural background of the person having them — a medieval Christian is unlikely to report an encounter with Waheguru, and a devout Sikh is unlikely to report seeing the Virgin Mary. This cultural conditioning, non-religious thinkers argue, suggests the experience originates in the human mind rather than in an external divine source. The appropriate response to claims of special revelation is, on this view, respectful scepticism and a search for natural explanations.

Key Fact

Four key divine attributes: omnipotent (all-powerful), omniscient (all-knowing), immanent (present within the world and in human experience), transcendent (beyond and above the universe). Most monotheistic traditions — Christianity, Islam, Judaism, Sikhism — hold that God is all four simultaneously. Some Hindu schools and Buddhist teachings describe the divine as impersonal rather than personal.
exam_tip_html:
On the 6-mark Explain question for this topic, a common mistake is confusing special and general revelation. Special revelation is direct and personal — a vision, a miracle, enlightenment. General revelation is indirect and universal — available to all through nature and scripture. You must be clear about which one you are describing. Always name a specific example of a vision (Saul on the road to Damascus, Acts 9; or Bernadette at Lourdes) and use it to explain WHY it counts as a source of knowledge about the divine. Remember to refer to a sacred writing or source of teaching — Acts 9, Qur’an 3:190, Genesis 1:31, or the Guru Granth Sahib are all strong sources for this lesson.

For the 12-mark Evaluate, make sure you engage with both sides of the argument about whether revelation is a reliable source of knowledge. Arguments for its value should reference believers’ experiences and their significance; arguments against should include Hume’s point about testimony, the cultural conditioning critique, and the possibility of natural (psychological) explanations. Your conclusion must say which side you find more persuasive, and why, with explicit reasoning.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Special revelation involves direct, personal encounters with the divine: visions (Saul on the road to Damascus, Acts 9; Bernadette at Lourdes) and enlightenment (the Buddha at Bodh Gaya; Guru Nanak’s revelation). These are understood differently across traditions — Buddhism’s enlightenment does not require a creator God.
  • General revelation — through nature and scripture (Genesis 1:31, Qur’an 3:190, Guru Granth Sahib) — is available to all and reveals divine attributes: omnipotent (all-powerful), omniscient (all-knowing), immanent (present in the world) and transcendent (beyond the universe).
  • Challenges include: contradictory revelations across traditions, the possibility that witnesses were lying or mistaken (Hume), psychological explanations for religious experiences, and the humanist view that religious experiences originate in the human mind rather than in an external divine source.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes 'general revelation'?
A) A personal vision or miracle experienced by one individual
B) Knowledge of God available to all through the natural world and scripture
C) The Buddhist teaching of enlightenment under the Bodhi tree
D) A direct communication from God to a specific prophet
practice_questions.marks: B) Knowledge of God available to all through the natural world and scripture [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name one example of a vision from the Christian tradition.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of the following accepted for 1 mark: Saul on the road to Damascus (Acts 9) (1); Bernadette Soubirous at Lourdes (1858) (1); the Virgin Mary appearing to Bernadette (1).

practice_questions.text: Give two contrasting ideas about whether God is personal or impersonal.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark per idea stated, 2 marks per idea developed. For example: Most Christian, Muslim, Jewish and Sikh traditions describe God as personal — a being who hears prayer, acts in history and cares for individuals (1); this is supported by texts such as Psalm 139 ('You have searched me, Lord, and you know me') which present God as intimately involved in individual human lives (2). By contrast, some Hindu schools such as Advaita Vedanta describe Brahman as ultimately impersonal — the ground of all existence without personal characteristics such as feelings or intentions (1); on this view, the highest spiritual goal is realising that the individual self (atman) is one with Brahman, rather than entering a personal relationship with a deity (2).

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why some believers find visions a convincing source of knowledge about God.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons, each explaining why visions count as convincing evidence of God. At least one specific vision example named and linked to a sacred text or source of authority. For example: reason 1 — the dramatic transformation of the person who had the vision (Saul/Paul in Acts 9 became the founding apostle of Christianity, a change so radical that believers see it as requiring a genuine divine cause); reason 2 — the corroborating physical evidence in some cases (the healings at Lourdes, recognised by medical scrutiny, suggest that something beyond natural explanation is occurring). Source(s) named and developed. Secure: Two relevant reasons; source referenced but partially developed. Developing: One reason developed; source vague or absent. Emerging: Basic point only; largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Tariq, a 17-year-old Muslim student, tells his Religious Studies class that he thinks the natural world is the best evidence for God. His classmate Rosa says she finds personal visions more convincing. Explain two reasons Tariq might give for his view.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark per reason stated, 2 marks per reason developed. For example: Tariq might argue that general revelation through nature is available to everyone, not just those who happen to have a vision (1); the Qur'an (3:190) says that in the creation of the heavens and earth 'there are signs for those who reason', suggesting that God intentionally made the natural world a source of knowledge accessible to all humanity (2). He might also argue that personal visions could be explained by psychology or cultural expectation (1), whereas the existence of the ordered universe is an objective fact that cannot be dismissed as an individual's subjective experience (2).

practice_questions.text:
'Visions and religious experiences are not a reliable source of knowledge about God.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to religious and non-religious views
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: Hume argued that it is always more probable a witness was mistaken or lying than that a miracle or vision genuinely occurred. Visions in different religious traditions produce contradictory descriptions of God (personal/impersonal, one God/many gods), suggesting they cannot all be accurate. Modern psychology can explain mystical experiences through unusual brain states, sensory deprivation or grief, without invoking the supernatural. Humanists and atheists argue that the content of religious experiences reflects the cultural background of the person, suggesting human origin rather than divine revelation.

Arguments against: Many who have had visions report life-transforming changes that are hard to explain naturally — Saul's conversion (Acts 9) is cited as evidence that something objective occurred. The Catholic Church subjects miracle claims at Lourdes to rigorous medical scrutiny before recognising them, and 70 have been recognised. General revelation through nature is corroborated by independent evidence across cultures and traditions. Many philosophers (William Alston, Alvin Plantinga) argue that religious experience is epistemically justified — just as we trust sense perception as a source of knowledge about the world, we may be justified in trusting religious experience. The Guru Granth Sahib and other scriptures represent tested, communal forms of revelation rather than idiosyncratic personal claims.

Mastering: Balanced evaluation; at least two points on each side developed; sources used (Acts 9, Qur'an 3:190, Genesis 1:31); non-religious views engaged with; justified conclusion present. Secure: Main points present; source referenced but not fully developed; conclusion reached but weighing incomplete. Developing: One-sided; limited source use; conclusion absent. Emerging: Descriptive only; no evaluation or conclusion.

options: Knowledge of God available to all through the natural world
Direct, personal communication from God to a specific individual
The study of divine attributes in theological texts
The belief that God is both immanent and transcendent

knowledge_checks.q: Which term describes God as present and active within the world and in human experience?
Saul's blinding vision on the road to Damascus is recorded in the book of _____ in the Bible.
Knowledge of God available to all through nature and scripture is called _____ revelation.
Match each divine attribute to its definition:
right: All-powerful; able to do anything that is logically possible
Existing beyond and above the physical universe, not limited by space or time
All-knowing; having complete knowledge of all things

flashcard_questions.a: Direct, personal communication or experience of God or ultimate reality, such as a vision, miracle or enlightenment.
Indirect knowledge of God available to all people through the natural world, reason and scripture.

flashcard_questions.q: What happened to Saul on the road to Damascus?
flashcard_questions.a: He was surrounded by a blinding light and heard the voice of Jesus; he was converted and became Paul the Apostle.

flashcard_questions.q: Who reported the visions at Lourdes in 1858?
flashcard_questions.a: Bernadette Soubirous, a 14-year-old girl who saw a luminous woman who identified herself as the Immaculate Conception.

flashcard_questions.q: What is enlightenment in the context of religion?
flashcard_questions.a: A profound experience of direct insight into ultimate reality; in Buddhism, the awakening of the Buddha at Bodh Gaya.
All-powerful; able to do anything that is logically possible.
All-knowing; having complete and unlimited knowledge of all things.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'immanent' mean when describing God?
flashcard_questions.a: God as present within the world and within human experience, active in history and in individuals' lives.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'transcendent' mean when describing God?
flashcard_questions.a: God as existing beyond and above the physical universe, not limited by space, time or matter.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a vision in a religious context?
flashcard_questions.a: A supernatural experience in which a person believes they see or hear God, a divine being or a messenger of God.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Hume's challenge to visions and miracle accounts?
flashcard_questions.a: It is always more probable that a witness was mistaken or lying than that the laws of nature were actually broken.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do humanists question visions as a source of knowledge about God?
flashcard_questions.a: They argue that the content of religious experiences reflects the cultural background of the person, suggesting human rather than divine origin.

glossary_terms.definition: Direct, personal communication or experience of God or ultimate reality, such as a vision, miracle or moment of enlightenment.
Indirect knowledge of God available to all people through the natural world, reason and scripture, rather than through a direct personal encounter.
A supernatural experience in which a person believes they see or hear God, a divine being, or a messenger of God.
A profound experience of direct insight into ultimate reality; in Buddhism, the awakening of the Buddha; in other traditions, a direct experience of union with or knowledge of God.
All-powerful; able to do anything that is logically possible; one of the key attributes ascribed to God in monotheistic religions.
All-knowing; having complete knowledge of all things, past, present and future.
A description of God as present within the world and within human experience, active in history and in individuals' lives.
A description of God as existing beyond and above the physical universe, not limited by space, time or matter.
A description of God as a being with whom humans can have a personal relationship, who cares for individuals and responds to prayer.

hero_image_caption: Across religious traditions, believers describe moments of direct encounter with the divine through visions, enlightenment and the beauty of the natural world.
